os-sacrum.summary: A triangular bone formed by the fusion of the five sacral vertebrae. It forms the back wall of the pelvis and makes the sacroiliac joints with the hip bones.
facts: Fusion of the 5 sacral vertebrae (S1–S5), complete at about 25 years
Promontory, anterior and posterior sacral foramina, median sacral crest, sacral hiatus, auricular surface, sacral canal, ala of the sacrum
L5 (lumbosacral joint), hip bones (sacroiliac joints), coccyx
Wider, shorter and less curved in women
clinical: Caudal anaesthesia into the epidural space through the sacral hiatus is used in obstetrics and paediatric surgery.
The promontory is an important landmark in obstetric pelvic measurements (true conjugate).
tus: The sacrum forms from five fused sacral vertebrae; the anterior rami of the sacral nerves leave through the anterior sacral foramina.
Weight passes to the pelvis through the sacroiliac joints; the promontory is the reference point for obstetric measurements.

os-coccygis.summary: A small triangular bone at the lowest end of the spine, formed by the fusion of 3–5 small rudimentary vertebrae.
facts: Fusion of 3–5 coccygeal vertebrae
Gluteus maximus, coccygeus, levator ani (anococcygeal ligament), sacrotuberous ligament
Sacrococcygeal joint with the sacrum
clinical: Falling onto the buttocks can fracture the coccyx or cause coccyx pain (coccydynia).
tus: Coccydynia (tailbone pain) usually follows a fall or childbirth.
The gluteus maximus, sacrotuberous ligament and part of the levator ani (anococcygeal ligament) attach to the coccyx.

sternum.summary: The flat, sword-shaped bone in the front midline of the thoracic cage. It articulates with the clavicles and the first seven pairs of costal cartilages.
facts: Flat bone (contains red marrow)
Manubrium, body, xiphoid process
Jugular notch, clavicular notches, sternal angle (angle of Louis – level of the 2nd rib), costal notches
Clavicle (sternoclavicular joint), 1st–7th costal cartilages (sternocostal joints)
sections: The junction of the manubrium and the body can be felt through the skin and marks the level of the 2nd costal cartilage. At this level (T4–T5) the aortic arch begins and ends and the trachea divides (tracheal bifurcation).
clinical: Bone marrow can be sampled from the sternum.
In open-heart surgery the sternum is split down the middle (median sternotomy).
Chest compressions (CPR) are given on the lower half of the sternum; pressure on the xiphoid process can injure the liver.
tus: The body of the sternum is used for sternal puncture; take care, as the great vessels and heart lie behind it.
The jugular notch of the manubrium lies at the lower border of T2, the xiphisternal joint at T9.

costae.summary: Twelve pairs of curved flat bones forming the side walls of the thoracic cage. They join the thoracic vertebrae at the back and the sternum at the front through their cartilages.
facts: 12 pairs: 1–7 true ribs, 8–10 false ribs, 11–12 floating ribs
Head, neck, tubercle, body (shaft), angle
Costal groove (on the lower border – intercostal vein, artery and nerve run here in VAN order), crest of the head
Ribs 1, 2, 10, 11 and 12; the 1st rib is the shortest, flattest and most curved (grooves for the subclavian artery and vein, scalene tubercle)
sections: In inspiration the upper ribs lift the sternum forwards and increase the anteroposterior diameter (pump-handle movement); the lower ribs swing outwards and increase the transverse diameter (bucket-handle movement).
clinical: Chest drains and thoracentesis go over the upper border of a rib to protect the intercostal vessels and nerve.
Several ribs broken in two places produce a flail chest with paradoxical breathing.
A cervical rib can compress the brachial plexus or subclavian artery and cause thoracic outlet syndrome.
tus: A typical rib has a head, neck, tubercle, angle and costal groove; ribs 1, 2, 10, 11 and 12 are atypical.
Rib fractures occur most often just in front of the angle; a flail chest is two fractures in each of several ribs.

cartilagines-costales.summary: Bars of hyaline cartilage that connect the front ends of the ribs to the sternum or to the cartilage above. They make the thoracic cage flexible.
facts: Hyaline cartilage
1–7: directly to the sternum; 8–10: to the cartilage above (costal margin); 11–12: free ends
May calcify in old age
clinical: Inflammation of the costochondral junctions (costochondritis, Tietze syndrome) can cause chest pain that mimics cardiac pain.
tus: The 1st costal cartilage forms a synchondrosis with the manubrium; cartilages 2–7 form synovial joints with the sternum.
Inflammation of a costochondral junction (Tietze syndrome) causes painful swelling and can mimic cardiac pain.

clavicula.summary: An S-shaped long bone lying horizontally between the sternum and the scapula. It is the only bony strut connecting the arm to the trunk.
facts: Long bone (no marrow cavity)
Sternal end (sternoclavicular joint) and acromial end (acromioclavicular joint)
Conoid tubercle, trapezoid line, impression for the costoclavicular ligament, groove for the subclavius
Deltoid, trapezius, pectoralis major, sternocleidomastoid, sternohyoid, subclavius
The first bone in the body to begin ossifying (weeks 5–6) and the last to finish
clinical: One of the most frequently fractured bones; the fracture is usually at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds. The medial fragment is pulled up by the sternocleidomastoid, the lateral fragment down by the weight of the arm.
In clavicle fractures the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels passing beneath it can be injured.
tus: Clavicle fractures are commonest in the middle third; the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus behind it are at risk.
The conoid tubercle and trapezoid line give attachment to the two parts of the coracoclavicular ligament.

scapula.summary: A triangular flat bone on the upper back of the thoracic cage, level with ribs 2–7. It forms the shoulder joint with the humerus and gives attachment to 17 muscles.
facts: Flat bone
Spine of the scapula, acromion, coracoid process, glenoid cavity, supraglenoid and infraglenoid tubercles, supraspinous fossa, infraspinous fossa, subscapular fossa, suprascapular notch
Humerus (glenohumeral joint), clavicle (acromioclavicular joint); functional scapulothoracic joint with the chest wall
Rotator cuff muscles, deltoid, trapezius, biceps brachii, triceps brachii, serratus anterior, rhomboids, levator scapulae, teres major, pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis, omohyoid
sections: Elevation, depression, protraction, retraction and upward/downward rotation. When the arm is raised overhead, about 1 degree in every 3 comes from rotation of the scapula (scapulohumeral rhythm).
clinical: If the long thoracic nerve is injured, the serratus anterior is paralysed and the medial border of the scapula lifts like a wing (winged scapula).
Entrapment of the suprascapular nerve at the suprascapular notch causes shoulder pain and weakness of supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
tus: Scapular landmarks: superior angle at T2, spine at T3, inferior angle at T7.
17 muscles attach to the scapula; a winged scapula indicates injury to the long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior).

humerus.summary: The single and longest bone of the upper arm. Above it forms the shoulder joint with the scapula, below the elbow joint with the radius and ulna.
facts: Long bone
Head, anatomical neck, surgical neck, greater and lesser tubercles, intertubercular sulcus
Deltoid tuberosity, radial groove
Capitulum, trochlea, medial and lateral epicondyles, olecranon fossa, coronoid fossa, radial fossa, groove for the ulnar nerve
Primary centre in the shaft at week 8; 8 secondary centres
sections: The humerus touches three important nerves directly: the axillary nerve at the surgical neck, the radial nerve in the radial groove of the shaft and the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle. Its fractures are therefore prone to nerve injury.
clinical: Fracture of the surgical neck: injury to the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery (deltoid paralysis).
Midshaft fracture: radial nerve injury – wrist drop.
Supracondylar fracture (common in children): injury to the brachial artery and median nerve, risk of Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.
Fracture of the medial epicondyle: ulnar nerve injury – claw hand.
tus: Three nerves contact the humerus: surgical neck – axillary nerve, shaft (groove) – radial nerve, medial epicondyle – ulnar nerve.
In supracondylar fractures the brachial artery and median nerve (especially the anterior interosseous nerve) can be injured.

radius.summary: The long bone on the lateral (thumb) side of the forearm. It turns around the ulna during pronation and supination and makes the main joint with the wrist.
facts: Long bone
Head, neck, radial tuberosity (biceps brachii attaches)
Radial styloid process, ulnar notch, carpal articular surface, dorsal tubercle (Lister's tubercle)
Humerus (humeroradial joint), ulna (proximal and distal radioulnar joints), scaphoid and lunate (radiocarpal joint)
Biceps brachii, supinator, pronator teres, brachioradialis, pronator quadratus, flexor pollicis longus, abductor pollicis longus
clinical: A fracture of the distal radius after a fall on the outstretched hand (Colles' fracture) is among the commonest fractures; the distal fragment shifts backwards, giving a 'dinner-fork' deformity.
In children a sudden pull on the arm can slip the radial head out of the annular ligament (pulled elbow).
tus: Radial head subluxation (pulled elbow) is common between 1 and 4 years.
Galeazzi fracture: radial shaft fracture + dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint; Monteggia: ulnar fracture + dislocation of the radial head.

ulna.summary: The long bone on the medial (little finger) side of the forearm. Its upper end forms the main hinge of the elbow with the humerus; the olecranon forms the point of the elbow.
facts: Long bone
Olecranon, coronoid process, trochlear notch, radial notch, ulnar tuberosity
Head of ulna, ulnar styloid process
Humerus (humeroulnar joint), radius (radioulnar joints)
Triceps brachii (olecranon), brachialis (ulnar tuberosity), flexor digitorum profundus, pronator quadratus, supinator, anconeus, flexor carpi ulnaris, extensor carpi ulnaris
clinical: Monteggia fracture: fracture of the upper third of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head.
In olecranon fractures the triceps pulls the proximal fragment up; surgical fixation is usually needed.
tus: In an olecranon fracture the triceps pulls the fragments apart; surgical fixation is needed.
A nightstick fracture (isolated ulnar shaft fracture) occurs when someone raises the forearm to shield the face.

ossa-carpi.summary: Eight short bones in two rows that form the wrist. The groove on their front (carpal sulcus) is roofed by the flexor retinaculum to form the carpal tunnel.
facts: Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform
Trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate
‘Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle’ (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate)
Median nerve and 9 tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL)
clinical: Carpal tunnel syndrome: compression of the median nerve causes numbness of the thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger and thenar muscle wasting.
Because the ossification centres appear in order with age, a wrist X-ray is used to estimate bone age.
tus: Of the carpal bones the capitate ossifies first and the pisiform last (used to estimate bone age).
Proximal row: Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform; distal row: Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate.

os-scaphoideum.summary: A boat-shaped bone at the lateral end of the proximal carpal row. It is one of the main bones articulating with the radius and the most frequently fractured carpal bone.
facts: Proximal row, most lateral; in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox
Radius, lunate, capitate, trapezium, trapezoid
Scaphoid tubercle (the flexor retinaculum attaches)
Branches of the radial artery; blood flows from distal to proximal
clinical: It breaks in a fall on the outstretched hand; tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is typical.
Because the blood supply comes from distal, fractures of the waist can lead to avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment; the first X-rays may be normal, so a cast is applied when in doubt.
tus: The most frequently fractured carpal bone; with snuffbox tenderness a cast is applied even if the X-ray is normal.
Since blood flows from distal to proximal, waist fractures carry a high risk of AVN of the proximal fragment.
